# Distillation of strong alcohol (aqua vitae) (`distillation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by fermentation_yeast, glassmaking, thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: Alcohol boils at 78 °C, water at 100 °C, so the first vapour from gently heated wine is richer in alcohol. Lead the vapour from a closed pot (cucurbit and still-head) through a long tube or coil that runs through cold water, and collect the drops. Wine of 10–13 % gives about 30–40 % on the first run and 60–70 % on the second; ordinary distillation at atmospheric pressure approaches an azeotrope of about 96 % ethanol by mass. A flame test cannot reliably measure alcohol strength. For disinfecting, 60–80 % works best.
- Pitfalls:
  - Heating too hard: everything boils over together and nothing is separated.
  - A blocked or sealed still bursts; the vapour and the spirit catch fire at an open flame.
  - Lead or lead-soldered still-heads and coils poison the spirit; use copper, glass or glazed ware.
  - Believing distillation creates alcohol. It only concentrates what fermentation made.
  - Thinking pure alcohol disinfects best; about 70 % kills more reliably than 95 %.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1200 BC – perfumers' texts (Tapputi) describe extraction and sublimation vessels; true distillation is uncertain; egypt: 1st–3rd c. AD – Alexandrian alchemists (Maria the Jewess, Zosimos) describe the still-head with receiver (ambix); india: c. 150 BC–AD 150 – pottery stills from Taxila and Shaikhan Dheri are argued to be for alcohol (Allchin); disputed; china: 12th–13th c. – distilled liquor certain under the Jin and Yuan; an Eastern Han bronze still is known but its use is disputed; islamic: 9th c. – al-Kindi distils perfumes and mentions distilled wine; al-Razi describes the apparatus; europe: 12th c. – aqua ardens at Salerno; c. 1280 Taddeo Alderotti describes aqua vitae and a water-cooled coil
- Read:
  - R. J. Forbes, A Short History of the Art of Distillation (1948)
  - Hieronymus Brunschwig, Liber de arte distillandi de simplicibus (1500)
